title: Web Security Essentials: TLS, Headers, Secrets and OWASP
summary: Quick revision notes on how TLS secures a connection, how certificates, HSTS and secure headers harden it, how to manage secrets and supply chain risk, and the OWASP Top 10 at a glance.

chapters.title: TLS Mental Model and Handshake
points: TLS gives three guarantees: confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tamper detection), authentication (the server proves identity via its certificate)
TLS 1.3 handshake: ClientHello (versions, ciphers, key share) → ServerHello + certificate + Finished → client Finished, so it takes 1 round trip
Key exchange is ephemeral (ECDHE) and gives forward secrecy: a stolen server key cannot decrypt past recorded sessions
Asymmetric crypto only authenticates and agrees on a key; bulk data uses a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20
Interview Point: Walk through a TLS 1.3 handshake. What is forward secrecy? Why not encrypt all data with the public key? What does TLS 1.3 remove versus 1.2?

chapters.title: Certificates and HSTS
points: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to a domain (SAN field) and is signed by a CA; the client checks the chain leaf → intermediate → trusted root, plus expiry and hostname match
Inspect a live server: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com; read the dates with openssl x509 -noout -dates
HSTS header Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload makes browsers force HTTPS and refuse click-through on cert errors
HSTS only takes effect after the first HTTPS visit unless the domain is on the preload list; the first plain HTTP request can still be intercepted (SSL stripping)
Interview Point: How does a browser validate a certificate chain? What does HSTS stop that a 301 redirect to HTTPS does not? What are the risks of preloading?

chapters.title: Secure Headers
points: Content-Security-Policy restricts script, style and frame sources, e.g. default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; it is the main defence against XSS impact
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops MIME sniffing; Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin limits URL leakage
Clickjacking: use CSP frame-ancestors 'none' (or the older X-Frame-Options: DENY) so the page cannot be framed
Cookie flags: Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (no JS access), SameSite=Lax or Strict (blocks most CSRF)
Interview Point: What does CSP protect against and why is 'unsafe-inline' a problem? Which cookie flags matter and why? How do you check headers with curl -I?

chapters.title: Secrets Management and Supply Chain Risks
points: Never commit secrets: keep .env in .gitignore and scan with gitleaks or trufflehog; a secret that reached git history is compromised, so rotate it, because deleting the commit is not enough
Load secrets at runtime from a manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, cloud KMS) or injected env vars, with least-privilege access, rotation and short-lived credentials
Dependency risks: known CVEs, typosquatting, dependency confusion (a public package shadowing an internal name), and malicious install scripts
Defences: commit lockfiles, pin versions, run npm ci, audit with npm audit or Dependabot, generate an SBOM, and verify package provenance and signatures
Interview Point: A key was pushed to GitHub, what do you do? What is dependency confusion? Why use a lockfile and npm ci in CI?

chapters.title: OWASP Top 10 at a Glance
points: A01 Broken Access Control (IDOR, missing authorization checks) is the top risk; enforce authorization server-side on every request, deny by default
A04 Cryptographic Failures and A06 Insecure Design (2025 numbering): plain HTTP, weak hashing, no threat modelling; hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2, never MD5 or SHA-1
A05 Injection (SQL, command, XSS): use parameterized queries and output encoding, never string-concatenate user input

A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures: default credentials, unpatched libraries, no MFA or rate limiting, unsigned updates

A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (SSRF now maps to A01): log auth events and alert on them; validate and allowlist outbound URLs to block metadata-endpoint access. Interview Point: Name 5 OWASP risks and a fix for each. What is IDOR? How do parameterized queries stop SQL injection?

chapters.title: Security Cheat Sheet
points: TLS: use 1.2 or 1.3 only, ECDHE for forward secrecy, auto-renew certificates (Let's Encrypt/ACME), include the full intermediate chain

Check commands: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host; curl -I https://host (look for Strict-Transport-Security and CSP); openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
Header baseline: Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, frame-ancestors; cookies Secure + HttpOnly + SameSite
Secrets and supply chain: no secrets in git, rotate on leak, least privilege, lockfile + npm ci, audit dependencies, minimal base images
Common mistakes: expired certs, mixed content, HSTS preload before all subdomains support HTTPS, wildcard CORS with credentials, verbose errors, trusting client-side checks
